title: Does time really slow down when you’re scared?
hook: In a scare, everything seems to go in slow motion. A free-fall experiment put that to the test.
summary: In a free-fall study, nobody gained slow-motion vision; the sense that time slowed comes later, in memory.

cardBlocks.text: Many people say that in an accident everything seemed to happen in slow motion. To test this, David Eagleman and colleagues took volunteers to a free-fall ride: they dropped backwards 31 metres into a net. On their wrists they wore a "perceptual chronometer" that flashed numbers too fast to read normally.

If time really slowed down, they would have been able to read the numbers during the fall. They couldn’t. Yet when asked afterwards how long their own fall had lasted, the volunteers estimated 36% longer than other people’s falls. The slow motion wasn’t in their perception, but in their memory.
In a scare, time doesn’t slow down; memory records the moment more richly, so it seems to have lasted longer.

deepDiveBlocks.text: The authors suggest that a frightening event is recorded more richly in memory. When it is recalled, that richness makes it seem to have lasted longer than it did.
For the researchers, subjective time is not a single thing that speeds up or slows down: it is made of parts that can work separately.

heroMedia.alt: Diagram of a backwards free fall into a net, with a wrist display flashing too fast to read; beside it, the memory of the fall holds more frames and seems longer than it was.
